---
title: Wildcards and Quoting
---

At the end of the last chapter we typed out `numbers/ten.txt numbers/twenty.txt`
to remove two files. Two was tedious. Twenty would have been unbearable.

This chapter is about naming a whole group of files at once. It introduces no
new commands - we will use `ls`, `echo`, `cp`, `mv` and `rm`, all of which we
already know. What is new is a pair of characters:

* `*` - stands for any number of characters
* `?` - stands for exactly one character

These are called **wildcards**. Along the way we will find out who actually
does the work when you type one, and that will lead us to quotes: the way to
tell the shell to leave your text alone.

## A place to work

Wildcards are about naming everything in a directory at once, so it matters
which directory you are standing in. We will work in one of our own, where a
mistake costs us nothing.

```session
$ cd
```

```session
$ mkdir wildcards
```

```session
$ cd wildcards
```

```session
$ pwd
/home/anand/wildcards
```

Now some files to practise on:

```session
$ seq 5 > five.txt
```

```session
$ seq 10 > ten.txt
```

```session
$ seq 20 > twenty.txt
```

```session
$ echo command line, files, wildcards > topics.md
```

`touch` takes more than one name at a time, just as `rm` did:

```session
$ touch day1.log day2.log day3.log day10.log
```

That gives us eight files:

```session
$ ls
day1.log   day2.log  five.txt  topics.md
day10.log  day3.log  ten.txt   twenty.txt
```

## Naming several files at once

Suppose we want to see only the `.txt` files. We can say so:

```session
$ ls *.txt
five.txt  ten.txt  twenty.txt
```

The `*` stands for any number of characters, so `*.txt` means "anything, as
long as it ends in `.txt`". The three number files match. `topics.md` does not,
and neither do the logs.

## What `*` matches

The `*` can go anywhere in the name. At the end, it matches everything that
starts a certain way:

```session
$ ls t*
ten.txt  topics.md  twenty.txt
```

Note that `topics.md` is in that list. We asked for names beginning with `t`
and said nothing at all about the ending.

At the start, it matches everything that ends a certain way:

```session
$ ls *y.txt
twenty.txt
```

And it can sit in the middle, fixing both ends and leaving the part between
free:

```session
$ ls day*.log
day1.log  day10.log  day2.log  day3.log
```

"Starts with `day`, ends with `.log`, anything in between."

One thing to be careful about: `*` matches *any number* of characters, and
that includes none at all. If we had a file called simply `day.log`, the
pattern `day*.log` would match it too.

## Who does the matching

Here is the question worth stopping on. When we type `ls *.txt`, does `ls` go
looking for files whose names end in `.txt`?

It does not. Watch:

```session
$ echo *.txt
five.txt ten.txt twenty.txt
```

`echo` knows nothing about files. All it ever does is print the arguments it is
given. So if `echo` printed three file names, those three names must have been
its arguments - they were already there by the time `echo` started.

That is exactly what happens. Before running the command, the shell looks at
`*.txt`, finds the names in the current directory that match, and replaces the
pattern with those names. The command that finally runs is:

```
echo five.txt ten.txt twenty.txt
```

`echo` never sees the `*`. Neither does `ls`, or `rm`, or any other command.
This is called **expansion**, and it is the shell's work, not the command's.

Try `*` on its own, which matches every name:

```session
$ echo *
day1.log day10.log day2.log day3.log five.txt ten.txt topics.md twenty.txt
```

This is why `echo` is the safest way to try out a pattern. It shows you exactly
what the shell will hand to a command, before you hand it to a command that
does something you cannot undo.

::: {.callout-tip}
Not sure what a pattern will match? Put `echo` in front of it and look.
:::

## Matching a single character with `?`

`?` stands for exactly one character - no more, no less.

```session
$ ls day?.log
day1.log  day2.log  day3.log
```

Three files, not four. `day10.log` has two characters where the `?` is, so it
does not match. Compare that with the `*` version from earlier:

```session
$ ls day*.log
day1.log  day10.log  day2.log  day3.log
```

That is the whole difference between the two. Use `?` when you know how long
the missing part is.

## Wildcards in paths

A wildcard can appear in any part of a path, not just the last. To try that, we
need a directory with something inside it. `mkdir` takes several names at once,
just as `touch` did:

```session
$ mkdir week1 week2 week3
```

Each one needs a file in it, with something we can recognise inside:

```session
$ echo the command line > week1/topics.txt
$ echo files and directories > week2/topics.txt
$ echo wildcards and quoting > week3/topics.txt
```

```session
$ ls
day1.log   day2.log  five.txt  topics.md   week1  week3
day10.log  day3.log  ten.txt   twenty.txt  week2
```

Three directories, each holding a `topics.txt`. A pattern can name them all:

```session
$ echo week*
week1 week2 week3
```

And a pattern can sit in the middle of a path, with a fixed name after it:

```session
$ echo week*/topics.txt
week1/topics.txt week2/topics.txt week3/topics.txt
```

Three paths. Now, since `cat` takes as many files as you give it:

```session
$ cat week*/topics.txt
the command line
files and directories
wildcards and quoting
```

Three files, from three directories, read with one short command. Nothing about
`cat` changed - the shell simply handed it three paths instead of one.

There is a rule hiding in this. A `*` never matches a `/`; it stays inside one
part of the path. That is why `*.txt` does not reach into the week directories:

```session
$ echo *.txt
five.txt ten.txt twenty.txt
```

The three `topics.txt` files are `.txt` files too, but they are one level down,
and `*` did not go looking for them. To reach them you have to say so, as we
did with `week*/topics.txt`.

## When nothing matches

What if a pattern matches nothing at all? The shell gives up and passes the
pattern through unchanged, exactly as you typed it:

```session
$ echo a*b
a*b
```

There is no file starting with `a` and ending with `b`, so there was nothing to
replace the pattern with, and `echo` printed the pattern itself.

This explains an error message that would otherwise be baffling:

```session
$ ls *.pdf
ls: cannot access '*.pdf': No such file or directory
```

`ls` is complaining about a file called `*.pdf`. It is not being obtuse. No
name matched, so the shell handed the pattern straight to `ls`, and `ls` did
the only thing it could - it looked for a file with that name.

So when you see a `*` inside an error message, read it as: nothing matched.

## Wildcards match names, not contents

`*.txt` does not mean "files with text in them". The shell never opens a single
file to work out what matches; it only compares names. A `.txt` file full of
nonsense matches, and a file full of beautiful prose named `topics.md` does
not.

Nor does a pattern care whether a name belongs to a file or a directory. When
we ran `echo week*`, the three things it matched were all directories.

## What this was all for

Back to the tedium we started with. Let's put the number files into a directory
of their own:

```session
$ mkdir numbers
```

```session
$ mv *.txt numbers/
```

```session
$ ls
day1.log   day2.log  numbers    week1  week3
day10.log  day3.log  topics.md  week2
```

```session
$ ls numbers
five.txt  ten.txt  twenty.txt
```

Three files moved with one command, and it would have been the same command for
three hundred. This is the pattern of the whole command line: you describe what
you want, and the number of files stops mattering.

## Look before you delete

`rm` accepts wildcards like everything else, which makes it the place to be
careful. `rm *.txt` is easy to type and impossible to undo, and if your finger
slips and it becomes `rm *`, you have removed everything in the directory.

So get into this habit: run the pattern past `ls` first, read the list, and only
then run `rm`.

```session
$ ls day*.log
day1.log  day10.log  day2.log  day3.log
```

That is the list we meant. Now press the up arrow to bring the line back, change
`ls` to `rm`, and press Enter:

```session
$ rm day*.log
```

```session
$ ls
numbers  topics.md  week1  week2  week3
```

::: {.callout-warning}
Watch out for a stray space. `rm * .log` is not `rm *.log` - it is two
arguments, and the first one is `*`, which matches everything. The space
changes "remove the log files" into "remove everything".
:::

## Turning the star off

Sometimes you want a `*` to be a plain star and nothing more. Try printing one:

```session
$ echo *
numbers topics.md week1 week2 week3
```

Not what we wanted. The shell expanded it before `echo` ever saw it. To stop
that, put it in quotes:

```session
$ echo '*'
*
```

```session
$ echo "*"
*
```

Quotes tell the shell that what is inside is plain text. No matching, no
expansion - the `*` is handed to `echo` as an ordinary character.

## What quotes really do

Stopping wildcards is only half of it. Try this:

```session
$ echo hello     world
hello world
```

We typed five spaces and got one. That is not `echo` tidying up. The shell
split the line into arguments wherever it found spaces, and handed `echo` two
of them: `hello` and `world`. `echo` printed them with a single space between,
because that is what `echo` does with two arguments. The extra spaces were
never part of anything.

Now with quotes:

```session
$ echo "hello     world"
hello     world
```

One argument this time, spaces and all. So the real rule is:

**Quotes make what is inside them a single argument, and stop the shell from
changing it.**

## Files with spaces in their names

This matters most with file names. Suppose we want a file called
`my notes.txt`:

```session
$ touch my notes.txt
```

```session
$ ls
my  notes.txt  numbers  topics.md  week1  week2  week3
```

We got **two** files - `my` and `notes.txt`. And that is fair enough: we handed
`touch` two arguments, so it made two files, exactly as it did when we typed
`touch day1.log day2.log day3.log day10.log`.

Let's clear them away and try again:

```session
$ rm my notes.txt
```

```session
$ touch "my notes.txt"
```

```session
$ ls
my notes.txt  numbers  topics.md  week1  week2  week3
```

One file, with a space in its name. Every command that touches it from now on
needs the quotes too:

```session
$ cat my notes.txt
cat: my: No such file or directory
cat: notes.txt: No such file or directory
```

```session
$ cat "my notes.txt"
```

The file is empty, so `cat` printed nothing - but it found it, which the
unquoted version could not.

A wildcard is another way to avoid the typing, since the shell fills in the
name for you, space and all:

```session
$ ls my*
my notes.txt
```

::: {.callout-tip}
You can put spaces in file names, but life is easier if you do not. Use
`my-notes.txt` or `my_notes.txt` and you will never have to think about
quoting the name again.
:::

## Single and double quotes

We have used both `'` and `"` and they behaved identically. For our purposes
they mostly do, and either one will serve you well.

There is one difference, and it will matter later. The shell keeps some values
under names, called **variables**. `HOME` is one of them: it holds the path to
your home directory. Writing `$` in front of the name asks for its value, and
the shell fills it in - another rewrite it does before the command runs, just
like a wildcard.

```session
$ echo $HOME
/home/anand
```

```session
$ echo "$HOME"
/home/anand
```

```session
$ echo '$HOME'
$HOME
```

Double quotes stopped the wildcard and the spaces, but let the variable
through. Single quotes stopped everything, and `$HOME` was printed exactly as
we typed it.

So: **double quotes stop wildcards and spaces but let `$` through; single
quotes stop everything.** There is more to say about variables, and we will
come back to them in a later chapter.

## Clearing up

Let's tidy away this chapter's directory, using wildcards to do it.

```session
$ pwd
/home/anand/wildcards
```

```session
$ ls
my notes.txt  numbers  topics.md  week1  week2  week3
```

The awkward name needs its quotes one last time:

```session
$ rm "my notes.txt"
```

Now the directories. `rmdir` only removes an empty directory, so the files
inside have to go first - and we can name both sets in one command:

```session
$ ls numbers
five.txt  ten.txt  twenty.txt
```

```session
$ rm numbers/* week*/topics.txt
```

```session
$ ls numbers
```

Empty, and so are the week directories. Now `rmdir` will take them, and it
accepts a wildcard like everything else:

```session
$ rmdir numbers week*
```

```session
$ ls
topics.md
```

One file left, and `*` will do for that:

```session
$ rm *
```

```session
$ ls
```

Now go up and remove the directory itself:

```session
$ cd ..
```

```session
$ rmdir wildcards
```

```session
$ ls wildcards
ls: cannot access 'wildcards': No such file or directory
```

Gone, and we know how to read that message now: there is nothing left of this
chapter's work.

Compare that clean-up with the one at the end of the last chapter, where we
named every file by hand.

## Summary

Wildcards:

| Pattern | What it matches |
|---------|-----------------|
| `*.txt` | any name ending in `.txt` |
| `t*` | any name starting with `t` |
| `day*.log` | starts with `day`, ends with `.log` |
| `?` | exactly one character |
| `day?.log` | `day1.log`, but not `day10.log` |
| `*` | every name in the directory |
| `week*/topics.txt` | one file in each matching directory |
| `echo *.txt` | shows what a pattern matches, safely |

Quotes:

| What you type | What the command gets |
|---------------|-----------------------|
| `echo *` | every file name |
| `echo '*'` | a single `*` |
| `echo hello   world` | two arguments, `hello` and `world` |
| `echo "hello   world"` | one argument, spaces kept |
| `touch "my notes.txt"` | one file with a space in its name |
| `echo '$HOME'` | the text `$HOME` |
| `echo "$HOME"` | your home directory |

And the one idea to carry forward: the shell rewrites your line before the
command runs. Wildcards are how you ask it to, and quotes are how you ask it
not to.
